title: Trustworthy External Command Execution knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Trustworthy External Command Execution”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Validating external inputs” under lesson 136, “Trustworthy External Command Execution”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Trustworthy External Command Execution”?
options: Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.answer_key: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.explanation: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Trustworthy External Command Execution”?
options: Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
questions.answer_key: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
questions.explanation: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
